lede: A magnet's pull reaches out into the space around it: its magnetic field. A compass can map that field, and a coil carrying a current makes the same field, one you can switch on and off. That is an electromagnet, and you will learn exactly what makes it stronger.
can: Draw and read the field lines of a bar magnet and of a coil
Find a coil's poles from its current, and its current from its poles
Name the three ways to make an electromagnet stronger or weaker

caption: Field lines leave the north pole and enter the south pole; they crowd together where the field is strongest.

md: Field lines show the field's shape and direction. Outside the magnet they run **from the north pole to the south pole**, with an arrow on every line. They never cross, and crowd **closest near the poles**, where the field is strongest. A **plotting compass** points its north end along a line, the way of the arrow.

Read the bar magnet in the figure:
**Which end do the lines leave?** The north end; they enter the south end.
**Which way do the needles point?** Along the lines, from north round to south.

prompt: A pupil draws the field lines curving over the top of a bar magnet and must add the arrows. Which way should they point?
options: from the north pole to the south pole
from the south pole to the north pole
answer: from the north pole to the south pole
explain: Look at the arrows round the bar magnet: every line leaves the north end, curves round and goes into the south end, and each compass needle points the same way. So outside the magnet the field runs from the north pole to the south pole.

caption: Mark where the needle points, move the compass on, and repeat: the dots make one field line.

md: A plotting compass is a tiny magnet: its needle lines up along the field line it sits on, its north end pointing the way of the arrow. Stepping it along from pole to pole traces one line. Iron filings show the shape quickly, but not the direction: only a compass gives that.

Worked, for the compasses in the figure:
1. Set the first compass beside the north pole and mark a dot where its north end points.
2. Move the compass on so its tail sits on that dot, and mark again.
3. Carry on to the south pole, then join the dots and add the arrow.

prompt: Compasses are placed one after another along a field line that runs from a bar magnet's north pole over to its south pole. Which way does each needle's north end point?
options: along the line, on towards the south pole
along the line, back towards the north pole
straight at the middle of the magnet
answer: along the line, on towards the south pole
explain: Look at the five compasses in the picture: each needle lies along the dashed line, and its filled north end points on towards the south pole, because the field runs from north to south outside the magnet. That is why each new dot is marked where the north end points. The answer is along the line, on towards the south pole.

md: A current in a coil makes a magnetic field. Outside, it is **shaped like a bar magnet's**, with a north and a south end; inside, the lines are **straight and parallel**, running from south to north. The current's direction decides which end is north.

alt: Two end views of a coil: on the left the current goes anticlockwise and the end is a north pole; on the right it goes clockwise and the end is a south pole.

caption: Look at one end: current going anticlockwise makes it a north pole; clockwise makes it a south pole.

md: To find the poles, look at one end and follow the current round: **anticlockwise** makes it a **north** pole, **clockwise** a **south** pole. The other end is the opposite pole.

Worked, for the two ends in the figure:
1. Left circle: the current goes anticlockwise, so that end is a north pole.
2. Right circle: the current goes clockwise, so that end is a south pole.

prompt: Seen from the left-hand end of a coil, the current flows anticlockwise. Which pole is the right-hand end?
options: no pole: only bar magnets have poles
explain: Use the end rule from the two circles: anticlockwise seen from the left-hand end makes that end a north pole, and the other end is always the opposite pole, so the right-hand end is a south pole. A coil carrying a current has poles just as a bar magnet does. So a clockwise current makes this end a south pole.

caption: Turn the cell round: every arrow reverses and the poles change ends, but the shape stays the same.

md: Turn the cell round and the current flows the other way through the coil. The field keeps exactly the same shape, but **every arrow reverses**, so the **north and south poles swap ends**. The field is no stronger and no weaker: the current's size has not changed, only its direction.

Compare the two coils in the figure:
1. As wired: north is at the left end.
2. Cell turned round: every arrow reverses, and north is now at the right end.

prompt: The current in a coil is reversed. What happens to its magnetic field?
options: the north and south poles swap ends
answer: the north and south poles swap ends
explain: Compare the two coils in the picture: with the cell turned round, each field arrow points the other way, so the pole that was on the left is now on the right. The same current flows, so the strength is unchanged. The answer is that the poles swap ends.

caption: The poles are known and the current is hidden: work out its direction at X.

md: The end rule works backwards too. Find the north end (the field lines leave it), look at the coil from an end, and choose the current that makes that pole: anticlockwise for north, clockwise for south. Inside the coil the field runs **from south to north**, so each line is a closed loop.

Worked from the right-hand end in the figure:
1. The field lines enter the right end, so it is a south pole.
2. From that end, a south pole needs the current clockwise.
3. From there the front of the coil is on your left, where clockwise runs upwards: at X the current flows up.

prompt: The field lines leave the right-hand end of a coil. Seen from that right-hand end, which way does the current flow?
options: it cannot be told from the field lines
explain: Field lines leave a north pole, so the right-hand end is north. The end rule, read backwards as in the worked lines: seen from a north pole, the current runs anticlockwise. The answer is anticlockwise.

caption: Three changes make an electromagnet stronger: more current, more turns and a soft iron core.

md: A coil with a core, used as a switchable magnet, is an **electromagnet**. Three changes make it stronger: **more current**, **more turns** of wire, and a **soft iron core**. The opposites make it weaker: less current, fewer turns, or taking the core out.

title: Why soft iron
md: Soft iron is strongly magnetised while the current flows and loses its magnetism when it stops, so the electromagnet can be switched off: that is how a scrapyard crane drops its load.

md: Say the quantity, not the part: 'a bigger battery' earns nothing, so write 'increase the current'. The core's size does not earn the mark; its material does. Most Summer 2025 answers lost these marks this way.

prompt: A question asks for a way to make an electromagnet stronger. Which answer earns the mark?
explain: The marks go to the three quantities in the picture: the current, the number of turns and a soft iron core. 'A bigger battery' names a part instead of the current, and a thicker core changes its size, not its material. The answer that earns the mark is increase the current.

title: GCSE Physics Revision "Electromagnets"
why: An electromagnet built and made stronger, one change at a time.

title: Watching it for CCEA
md: The video is made for another exam board. If it goes on to the motor effect, Fleming's left-hand rule or relays, stop there: they are not on the CCEA Double Award specification.

Three changes that make an electromagnet weaker [3], written for full marks:
**First.** Decrease the current.
**Second.** Wind fewer turns of wire.
**Third.** Remove the iron core.

prompt: A question asks for three ways to decrease an electromagnet's strength. Which answer earns all three marks?
options: less current, fewer turns, take out the iron core
a smaller battery, a shorter core, fewer turns
more current, more turns, a soft iron core
answer: less current, fewer turns, take out the iron core
explain: Each mark is one of the three quantities, turned the right way: less current, fewer turns and no iron core. 'A smaller battery' and 'a shorter core' name a part or a size, so only 'fewer turns' would score in that answer, and the last answer makes the magnet stronger. The answer is less current, fewer turns, take out the iron core.

md: **Stronger or weaker?** Summer 2019 and 2023 asked how to increase the strength; Summer 2025 asked how to decrease it. Read which before you write.
**A core that is not iron.** An electromagnet drawn on a wooden core (Summer 2023) gets stronger when the wood is swapped for soft iron.

**The nails investigation.** Booklet B (Summer 2021) changed the current and counted the iron nails held:
**Changed.** The current.
**Measured.** The nails held, twice at each current, then averaged.
**Kept the same.** The turns and the core.

Worked first on a coil lifting paper clips as its core is changed:
**What is changed on purpose?** The core: independent.
**What is counted each time?** The paper clips: dependent.

prompt: A pupil changes the current through an electromagnet and counts the iron nails it holds. What is the dependent variable?
explain: The dependent variable is the one measured each time, as in the investigation above: the number of nails held. The current is the one changed on purpose, so it is the independent variable, and the turns are kept the same. The answer is the number of nails held.

Map a field line with a plotting compass, and say why filings cannot show direction.
Find a coil's poles from its current, or its current from its poles; say what reversing does.

P2 asks for the compass [1], the correct field drawing or arrows on field lines [1–3], the poles of a coil [1–3], and three ways to make an electromagnet stronger or weaker [3]. The marks for strength are for current, turns and a soft iron core, stated precisely. Stuck? Write current, turns, core.
